title: solar industry grapples with cutting its growing waste stream  ecmii 2026 08 11
text:
August 4 - There were 2.4 terawatts of solar PV generating electricity around the world at the end of 2025 – enough to power more than one billion homes. While it took nearly 70 years to reach the first terawatt, it took just two for the second – such is the pace of the technology’s expansion that the International Energy Agency believes it will account for 80% of the 4,600 gigawatts of renewable energy deployed between 2025 and 2030.
But that success has led many to question what will happen to all the panels once they break, or are replaced with newer technology, or eventually just lose efficiency?
Solar panels contain valuable materials, including silver, silicon, copper and glass, but also hazardous ones such as lead and cadmium. Recovering metals from end-of-life solar panels could generate around $6 billion a year by 2040, according ​to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA).
These recovered materials could supply around 70% of the silver needed to supply the growth of PV, and 20% of aluminium and copper, it said.
End-of-life solar PV treatment and recycling facilities are already operating in several major markets, including the EU, China and the United States.
Recycling of PV panels is mandatory in ‌the European Union, where it has come under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) directive since 2014. This targets the collection of 85% of end-of-life panels, and reuse or recycling of 80% of these, financed via a guarantee paid for by producers.
In China – the world’s biggest producer of solar PV technology – the government in 2023 introduced a requirement for plant owners to take the responsibility for the collection and treatment of end-of-life panels. Many Chinese solar PV manufacturers have established pilot recycling projects.
Typically, aluminium frames are removed and remelted, after which the remaining glass with silver, silicon and a fraction of plastics is typically shredded for uses such as glass wool in building insulation.
However, there is an increased focus on making the sector more circular as expansion continues apace. IRENA has forecast that global waste from the sector will rise from 0.2 megatonnes in 2021 to 4Mt in 2030, almost 50Mt in 2040 and more than 200Mt by 2050.
Ute Collier, deputy director of IRENA’s knowledge, policy ​and finance centre, said that while the combined capacity of existing facilities may be sufficient to deal with the current waste stream, dealing with end-of-life panels will be another story.
“When decommissioned solar PV panels are widely dispersed (geographically), and available in limited amounts, the market value of recovered materials may not be enough to cover the collection and processing costs,” she says.
Several governments, including ​the EU, India, Republic of Korea, South Africa, Singapore and state-level governments in the U.S. have introduced extended producer responsibility (EPR) policies to clarify who pays for collection, she notes.
However, others in the industry question IRENA’s forecast for waste volumes, arguing that PV panels are lasting far longer than expected.
Jan Clyncke ⁠managing director of PV CYCLE, which collects PV waste for recycling on behalf of solar farm operators, says an earlier IRENA forecast for waste volumes, in 2007, was the reason he founded PV Cycle.
“What a prognosis it had! … But what was predicted in 2007 hasn’t actually come through yet, 20 years later,” he says.
Since it started operations in 2010, PV Cycle has collected a total of 135,000 metric tons of ​PV waste – roughly the equivalent of 2 gigawatts, he says. This compares with some 450GW of solar PV now installed across Europe.
In 2025, it collected the highest amount, at 25,000 metric tons, but such volumes are still too low to interest recyclers, he says.
Solar is a very hard sector to predict volumes and timescales of waste, particularly for equipment used on residential rooftops, which householders will continue to use as long ​as they are generating sufficient electricity for their needs, he says.
An active debate in the solar industry is the extent to which PV panels should be designed to be easier to recycle. The EU is developing a system for scoring PV panels and inverters on their recyclability as part of a strategy to improve the recovery of critical raw materials from this waste stream.
The main barrier for PV-specific recycling is the low volume of PV modules available for recycling, and the distributed nature across EU member states.
And from a technical perspective, a key challenge to recovering materials at a high quality is the encapsulant, essentially a glue keeping the PV cells inside safe from moisture and other types of weathering, according to Christina Huber, senior policy advisor on sustainability for trade body Solar Power Europe.
“There’s been conversations about making the encapsulant easier to take apart, but the idea is that this equipment lasts outside for 30 years. Recyclability has to be ​taken hand-in-hand with durability. It’s all about resource use,” she says.
Henry Hielsmair, principal engineer for solar at technical advisory firm DNV, agrees. “People are focused on recycling to minimise waste, but the biggest lever to achieve that is to make modules last longer. But that isn’t necessarily compatible with making them recyclable.”
PV modules could be made to last 40 years, which is now expected in utility projects, instead of the current expectations ​of 25 to 30, but that will not happen unless manufacturers can price them to reflect quality, he says. “I think there’s a lot of modules going into the field that aren’t going to last as long as they’re expected to, and that’s a big problem,” he says.
Huber dismisses criticism from some in the sector that closed-loop recycling is not yet mainstream. The European sector is already further ahead than other industries, with its 85% weight-based ‌recycling in place sustainability minded, ⁠she says.
“The circular economy is not only about making new PV modules out of old PV modules, it’s about making sure that the resources keep going in a different product – this is also the circular economy,” she says.
However, volumes of waste will rise at some point, Huber acknowledges. Regulation needs to be reformed so that recycling businesses have confidence to make investments into PV-specific recycling infrastructure, capable of recovering the raw materials at a high quality now to ensure they have capacity to deal with it, she says.
She cites the example of the EU Waste Shipment Regulation, which is often a barrier to moving PV modules between countries, and establish regional recycling hubs for solar PV.
This year will be crucial for addressing barriers to PV recycling, with the revision of the WEEE directive under the EU’s Circular Economy Act, she believes. Huber is confident that solar PV will be given its own category and rules so that recovery of critical raw materials and higher value components contained in PV panels is incentivised.
Reuse of panels is a “largely untapped opportunity”, with many components of decommissioned solar PV panels having potential for repair, refurbishment and reuse, according to Collier.
However, reused solar PV panels and components must undergo proper inspection, testing and certification before they enter into the second-hand markets, ​and there is a need for a robust quality infrastructure system, she says.
The Chinese government is targeting ​recycling and reuse of over 250,000 metric tons of end-of-life solar PV panels by 2027, ⁠with an eye to large-scale decommissioning by 2030, she adds. In March, it published national guidance to promote the circular economy for solar panels, including reducing waste via green design and manufacturing, and encouraging the development of innovative technologies for recycling and reuse.
Warranties for solar PV modules typically cover them for 25-30 years until they are at 80% capacity, according to Huber. Though theoretically the product could last much longer, big utilities might be more interested in repowering with new technology, which would enable them to produce more energy on less space, she says.
“It’s definitely opening up the conversation towards reuse, but reuse is a niche ​because it comes with all kinds of other quality and warranty questions, and is facing competition from newer PV modules that are more efficient and very affordable,” she says.
For some, concerns over the solar sector’s impending waste stream are taken out of context. Hielsmair argues that the rollout of ​sufficient PV needed to reach 2050 climate change targets will ⁠already mean a significant reduction in energy-related waste, with volumes “orders of magnitude” smaller than those from coal-fired power plants, and other waste streams such as plastic and e-waste.
Treating waste from solar as an “environmental catastrophe” and banning landfill due to concerns about toxicity, as has been proposed in some U.S. states, will just worry communities, and delay the rollout of solar, he argues.
“I read an article that argued that we can’t leave our children with millions of metric tons of PV waste. But we are going to leave them with something. Make no mistake – I would rather them have a big pile of glass modules than the other impacts we're going to have if we don't deploy renewables,” he says.
SOLARCYCLE has developed technology to de-frame and de-glass PV panels for recycling at five sites around the U.S. It has developed the first-ever solar module made with ⁠50% recycled glass from end-of-life ​panels. In January, it partnered with ENGIE North America to introduce a “pre-cycling” provision in power purchase agreements for four projects to ensure that around one million panels from 375 megawatts (MW) of projects across the U.S. Midwest are recycled when they reach the ​end of their life.
French industrial cleantech company ROSI Solar has developed a process to recover high-purity strategic raw materials, including silicon and silver, as well as copper, aluminium and glass from solar panels. In April, it announced that it had secured more than 20 million euros to accelerate the rollout of its industrial projects, including its first fully standardised production line in Spain.
U.S.-based First Solar claims to be the only solar manufacturer with global in-house PV recycling capabilities, with a process that recovers more than 90% ​of module materials, including semiconductors, for reuse, providing high-quality secondary resources for new solar panels, glass, rubber and aluminium products.
A solar PV recycling facility owned by a subsidiary company of the Chinese state-owned State Power Investment Corporation entered commercial operation in March 2026, with capacity to process over 5,000 metric tons of end-of-life solar PV panels a year. It has already supplied 120 tons of recovered materials back to the market.
